title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • Write with clarity and precision.
  • Structure a paragraph so it argues rather than reports.
  • Integrate sources actively using the 'voices' technique.
  • Apply the four pillars as a self-review checklist.
  • Adapt your register to the genre a task requires.

title: Overview and justification
body: This course builds on the basics of getting a draft down. Here, the focus shifts to argument: how to make your writing not just correct, but persuasive - clear at the sentence level, structured at the paragraph level, and evidenced through the sources you bring in.

title: Signpost
body: This course moves through five techniques that build on each other, from sentence-level clarity to genre awareness.
instruction: Select each step to see what it covers.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: use the SVO model to identify and cut non-essential text, and shift sentences from passive to active voice for clarity.

title: Orientation
body: Academic writing gains power from every word that earns its place. Dense, wandering sentences bury the point you're trying to make; readers lose track of who did what to whom, and your argument slips past them. This lesson focuses on the sentence as your unit of control. You'll learn where to cut, where to reorder, and how changing voice (active or passive) sharpens meaning. These techniques are quick to learn, and the results show up in the very next piece of writing you edit.

title: Concept introduction
body:
Compare these two sentences:

A significant reduction in concentration levels can be caused by the constant use of mobile devices.

Constant mobile device use significantly reduces concentration.

The second is 7 words; the first is 16. Both say the same thing. What changed? The second sentence follows Subject–Verb–Object order: the thing doing the action (constant mobile device use) comes first, followed by what it does (significantly reduces), then what it affects (concentration). The first sentence buries the subject at the end and wraps the verb in passive padding ('can be caused by').

This is the SVO model: put your subject upfront, attach a strong verb directly to it, and let the sentence run forward. Passive voice inverts that order, often hiding who or what is doing the action. Sometimes you'll need the passive (when the actor is unknown, irrelevant, or less important than the object), but active voice is the default for clear, direct prose. The habit to build is simple: when you edit, find the actor, move it to the front, and let the verb carry the weight.

title: Practical guidance
body:
When you sit down to edit a draft, the SVO model gives you a diagnostic you can run on any sentence that feels bloated or unclear. Ask three questions:

  1. Who or what is doing something in this sentence?
  2. Is that actor at the front, or buried in a prepositional phrase?
  3. Is the verb direct, or wrapped in passive structure?

If the actor is buried, pull it forward. If the verb is passive and there's no good reason for it, flip the sentence to active voice. Most of the time, the rewritten version will be shorter, sharper, and easier to follow.

One caution: this is a reflex to build, not a rule to apply mechanically. Passive voice has its uses (when you want to emphasise the object, when the actor is genuinely irrelevant, when you're describing a convention). The goal isn't to eliminate every passive construction; it's to make the choice deliberately. Edit for clarity, not for a formula.

title: Formative check: active voice
body: Which sentence uses active voice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these three sentences uses active voice?

_items.text: The committee approved the proposal.
The proposal was approved by the committee.
Approval of the proposal occurred following committee review.

_feedback.correct: That's right. 'The committee approved the proposal' follows SVO order: the actor (committee) comes first, then the action (approved), then what's affected (proposal). This is active voice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the sentence where the actor comes first, before the verb. Which sentence has a clear subject doing the action?
_incorrect.final: 'The committee approved the proposal' is active voice because it follows SVO order: the committee (subject) approved (verb) the proposal (object). 'The proposal was approved by the committee' inverts this, putting the object first and the actor last; that's passive. 'Approval of the proposal occurred following committee review' buries both the actor and the action in nominalisations.

title: Summary
body: Clear academic writing depends on deliberate choices at the sentence level. This lesson introduced three techniques that work together: the SVO model (subject–verb–object order) as a structural default; the shift from passive to active voice to make your actor visible; and cutting non-essential text to let your main point land. Each applies during editing, not drafting: write freely first, then go back sentence by sentence and ask whether the reader can see who did what to whom. The sentences that survive that test are the ones that carry your argument.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: open a paragraph with a clear topic sentence, arrange supporting material in a logical order, and close with a sentence that states what the evidence shows.

title: Orientation
body: A well-structured paragraph does more than organise information; it makes your argument visible. When readers encounter a paragraph, they expect a clear claim at the start, evidence in the middle, and some sense of what the evidence means at the end. If those elements appear in the wrong order, or if the claim is buried halfway through, readers have to reconstruct your logic for themselves. This lesson focuses on the paragraph as your unit of argument: how to open it, how to arrange its contents, and how to close in a way that advances your case.

title: Concept introduction
body:
Consider what a reader expects when they start a new paragraph. They want to know, immediately, what point this paragraph will make. If the point only emerges at the end, they have to re-read to understand it; if it never emerges at all, they're left to guess.

A well-structured paragraph has three parts. The topic sentence opens by stating the claim or focus. The body provides evidence, arranged in a sequence that makes sense (chronological, logical, or from strongest to weakest). The close draws a conclusion: it doesn't just stop, it tells the reader what the evidence adds up to. This closing sentence is what distinguishes a paragraph that argues from one that merely reports.

The pattern is simple: claim → evidence → judgement. The claim tells the reader what you're arguing in this paragraph. The evidence supports it. The judgement connects that evidence back to your larger argument, saying explicitly what it shows. Without the judgement, you've assembled information but haven't done anything with it.

title: Worked example: structuring a paragraph
body: Here is a paragraph before and after restructuring. Select each heading to see how the same facts become an argument when given a clear structure.
instruction: Select each heading to compare the versions.

_items.title: The unstructured passage
_items.body:
Mobile phones are used constantly by students. Some studies show effects on concentration. There is also research on sleep. Universities have started offering guidance on screen time. It's a complicated area with many different findings.

Five sentences, five facts, no argument. The reader learns that things exist but not what the writer thinks about them. There's no opening claim, no logical sequence, and no conclusion.

_items.title: After: claim, evidence, judgement
_items.body:
Constant mobile phone use appears to affect student concentration and sleep. Several studies link frequent device use to reduced attention span during study sessions, while separate research connects screen time before bed to disrupted sleep patterns. In response, a number of universities have begun offering guidance on managing screen time. Taken together, this research suggests that mobile phone habits are a meaningful, addressable factor in academic performance.

Same facts, different structure. The first sentence states the claim; the middle sentences provide evidence in a logical sequence (attention, then sleep, then institutional response); the final sentence draws the conclusion. The paragraph now argues.

title: Practical guidance
body:
When you're editing a draft, you can audit any paragraph by asking three questions:

  1. Does the first sentence tell the reader what this paragraph is about?
  2. Is the supporting material arranged in an order that makes sense, or does it jump around?
  3. Does the final sentence state what the evidence shows, or does the paragraph just stop?

If the answer to any of these is no, restructure. Move your claim to the front if it's buried. Re-order your evidence so each sentence follows logically from the last. Add a closing sentence that draws the conclusion explicitly, even if it feels obvious to you; what's obvious to the writer is often invisible to the reader.

One clarification: the judgement at the end of a paragraph is not the same as the judgement at the end of an essay. It's local, not global. It says what this evidence shows for this point. The essay-level conclusion comes later; each paragraph's close feeds into it.

title: Formative check: topic sentence position
body: Which sentence is best placed as the OPENING of a paragraph?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these three sentences is best placed as the opening of a paragraph?

_items.text: Regular exercise has a measurable effect on academic performance.
For example, one study found a 15% improvement in test scores among students who exercised three times a week.
This suggests that physical activity should be considered part of an effective study routine.

_feedback.correct: That's right. 'Regular exercise has a measurable effect on academic performance' states the claim upfront, which is where the topic sentence belongs. It tells the reader what the paragraph is about before the evidence arrives.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The opening sentence should state the paragraph's main claim. Which sentence does that, rather than providing evidence or drawing a conclusion?
_incorrect.final: 'Regular exercise has a measurable effect on academic performance' is the topic sentence because it states the claim. 'For example, one study found...' is evidence supporting that claim, so it belongs in the body, not the opening. 'This suggests that...' is a concluding judgement, so it belongs at the end. All three sentences have a place in the paragraph, but only the claim belongs at the start.

body: Pick a paragraph you've written recently. Does the first sentence tell the reader what the paragraph is about, or do they have to read to the end to find out?
instruction: If you'd like, jot down your thoughts below. This is for your own reflection and won't be marked. Select Submit to save your response; it'll be here when you return.

title: Summary
body: A paragraph that argues has a visible structure: a topic sentence that states the claim, evidence arranged in a logical order, and a closing sentence that draws the conclusion. These three elements turn a collection of facts into a single point. The habit to build is simple: when you edit, check that each paragraph opens with its claim, sequences its evidence, and closes with its judgement. If any of those pieces is missing or misplaced, the paragraph drifts; fix it, and your argument sharpens.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: use the 'voices' technique to integrate sources actively into a paragraph, opening and closing with your own argument rather than simply reporting what sources say.

title: Orientation
body: Sources aren't decoration; they're the voices you bring into your argument. But bringing them in effectively is harder than it looks. Too often, students cite a source and let it speak for itself, reporting what someone found without saying what it means for their own argument. The result reads like a summary rather than an argument. This lesson focuses on the paragraph as a conversation: your voice opens, sources speak, and your voice closes. You'll learn a technique that keeps your argument in control while still doing justice to the evidence. The difference shows up immediately, because readers can finally hear your point, not just the sources you've gathered.

title: Concept introduction
body:
Consider a paragraph from a student essay:

Chen (2023) found that students working over 15 hours a week reported higher stress and lower engagement with coursework. Osei and Bramwell (2022) argue that structured part-time work can improve time-management skills and reduce anxiety around post-graduation employment.

Two sources, clearly cited. But what does the student think? The paragraph reports what researchers found without saying what it means. The writer's voice is absent.

Now consider what happens when the writer's voice frames the sources:

The relationship between part-time work and student wellbeing is not straightforward.

This opening sentence makes a claim. The sources that follow support, challenge, or complicate it. And a closing sentence will state what the writer concludes from the evidence.

This is the 'voices' technique: your voice opens the paragraph with a claim, source voices speak in turn, and your voice closes with a judgement. Think of it as a conversation you're chairing. You set the agenda, let others speak, then summarise what their contributions mean. Without that framing, your paragraph becomes a list of findings; with it, the paragraph argues.

title: Worked example: the voices technique
body: Here is a paragraph built step by step using the 'voices' technique. Select each heading to see how the paragraph takes shape, with each voice playing its role.
instruction: Select each heading to follow the four-step build.

_items.title: Step 1: Author's voice (opening)
_items.body:
The relationship between part-time work and student wellbeing is not straightforward.

The writer opens with a claim in their own voice. This sentence tells the reader what point the paragraph will make. It frames everything that follows.

_items.title: Step 2: Source A's voice
_items.body:
Chen (2023) found that students working over 15 hours a week reported higher stress and lower engagement with coursework.

The first source voice enters. This evidence supports one side of the claim: that part-time work can have negative effects. The writer hasn't commented yet; the source is doing the evidential work.

_items.title: Step 3: Source B's voice (contrast)
_items.body:
However, Osei and Bramwell (2022) argue that structured part-time work can improve time-management skills and reduce anxiety around post-graduation employment, provided hours stay within a manageable range.

A second source voice enters, offering a contrasting perspective. The word 'however' signals the shift. This evidence complicates the picture, supporting the writer's opening claim that the relationship is not straightforward.

_items.title: Step 4: Author's voice (closing judgement)
_items.body:
The evidence suggests that the effect of part-time work depends less on whether a student works than on how much, pointing to hours worked - not employment status alone - as the more useful variable for future research.

The writer's voice returns to close the paragraph. This sentence doesn't just summarise what the sources said; it draws a conclusion. The writer states what the evidence, taken together, shows. The paragraph now argues, rather than merely reports.

title: Practical guidance
body:
When you're editing a paragraph that cites sources, run this check:

  1. Is your opening sentence a claim you've made, or does it start with a source?
  2. Do the sources in the middle support, challenge, or complicate your claim, or are they just listed?
  3. Does the final sentence draw a conclusion in your voice, or does the paragraph end with the last source?

If your paragraph opens with 'Smith (2023) found that...' and ends with another source, your voice is missing. Pull back: what point are you making with these sources? State it at the start. Then let the sources speak. Then close by saying what, taken together, the evidence shows.

One note: this doesn't mean every paragraph needs multiple sources. A single source can work, as long as you frame it. The technique is about control, not quantity. Your voice opens, your voice closes; the sources do their work in between.

title: Formative check: writer's voice position
body: In the 'voices' technique, where should the writer's OWN view appear in the paragraph?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: In the voices technique, where should the writer's own view appear in the paragraph?

_items.text: At the start and the end, framing the sources in between.
Only at the end, after all sources have been presented.
Nowhere - the paragraph should let the sources speak for themselves.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Your voice opens the paragraph with a claim and closes it with a judgement. The sources speak in between, but you frame them. This keeps your argument in control.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about where the paragraph's claim and conclusion come from. Whose voice should open and close the paragraph?
_incorrect.final: Your voice should appear at the start and the end, framing the sources in between. The opening states your claim; the close draws your conclusion. If you only appear at the end, the reader doesn't know what point you're making until they've finished reading. If you don't appear at all, you're summarising others rather than arguing yourself.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look at a paragraph where you've cited sources. Are you reporting what they say, or using them to support a point you've already made?
instruction: If you'd like, jot down your thoughts below. This is for your own reflection and won't be marked. Select Submit to save your response; it'll be here when you return.

title: Summary
body: Integrating sources effectively means keeping your voice in control. The 'voices' technique structures each paragraph as a conversation: your opening sentence states the claim, source voices provide evidence (supporting, challenging, or complicating it), and your closing sentence draws the conclusion. Without that framing, your paragraphs report what others found; with it, they argue. The habit to build is simple: when you edit a paragraph that cites sources, check that your voice opens and closes. If the sources speak first and last, pull back and ask what point you're making.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: apply the four pillars of effective writing - clarity, structure, engagement with discourse, and presentation - as a self-review checklist to your own work.

title: Orientation
body: You have now worked through the core techniques of clear academic writing: SVO order and active voice for clarity, topic sentences and structured paragraphs for flow, and the voices technique for integrating sources. These techniques map onto four broader categories - what we will call the four pillars of effective writing: clarity, structure, engagement with discourse, and presentation. This lesson brings them together as a single, practical self-review checklist you can run on any piece of your own work before submission.

title: Concept introduction
body:
The four pillars recur across every genre of academic writing and appear in marking criteria across disciplines. They provide a reliable checklist for self-review:

  1. Clarity and precision of expression - say what you mean, no more and no less. If a sentence is not clear to you, it will not be clear to your reader.
  2. Structure - effective writing is organised. Plan carefully, use paragraphs deliberately, and think about how they connect.
  3. Effective engagement with relevant discourse - most assessed work requires you to draw on sources. Do not just report what you have found; show how it relates to your argument and why it matters.
  4. Presentation - this includes formatting (font, spacing, layout) and referencing. Small details here affect the overall impression your work makes.

These four pillars apply regardless of whether you are writing an essay, a report, or a reflective piece. They are also the categories most tutors use when marking, which makes them a practical self-check before submission (Dennis and Abbott, 2025).

title: Four pillars review
body:
Below is a sample paragraph. Select each pillar to see how it applies as a review lens.

Group projects is a good way for students working together and it can be really useful sometimes but there are also issues that come up like when people don't communicate well and this can affect the whole team's mark which happens quite often especially with big groups, see Robbins (2021) who talks about this a lot in his research on team dynamics generally.
instruction: Select each pillar to see the review.

_items.title: Clarity and precision
_items.body: This sentence runs to 65 words with three separate ideas stapled together. 'Is a good way' and 'can be really useful sometimes' say almost nothing - vague filler where a specific claim belongs. Clarity means saying exactly what you mean: which issue, how often, with what effect.

_items.title: Structure
_items.body: The paragraph lacks a topic sentence - the reader cannot tell what it is about until they have read the whole thing. No clear claim, evidence, judgement sequence. It reads as one long thought rather than a structured paragraph.

_items.title: Engagement with discourse
_items.body: Robbins (2021) is mentioned but not used - 'talks about this a lot' reports that a source exists without saying what it found or why it matters. This is citation without engagement.

_items.title: Presentation
_items.body: The citation format itself needs checking against the required style - 'see Robbins (2021) who talks about...' is not a standard in-text citation format. Small presentation details like this affect the overall impression, even when the content is sound.

title: Practical guidance
body:
When you are editing a draft, the four pillars give you a systematic way to review your own work before anyone else sees it. Work through them one at a time:

Start with clarity: read each sentence aloud. If you stumble, the reader will too. Ask whether every word earns its place.

Then check structure: does each paragraph open with a clear topic sentence? Does the evidence follow logically? Does the paragraph close with a judgement?

Next, engagement: for every source you cite, check that you are using it, not just reporting it. What does it show? Why does it matter for your argument?

Finally, presentation: check formatting against requirements, run through your references for consistency, and look at the document as a reader would see it.

This order - clarity, structure, engagement, presentation - mirrors the way most markers read. Strong content poorly presented can still lose marks; solid presentation without substance will not save weak work. Both matter.

title: Formative check: four pillars
body: A paragraph makes a strong claim but never cites any evidence for it. Which of the four pillars does this problem relate to?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A paragraph makes a strong claim but never cites any evidence for it. Which of the four pillars does this problem relate to?

_items.text: Engagement with relevant discourse
Clarity and precision of expression
Presentation

_feedback.correct: That is right. When a claim is not supported by evidence, the issue is engagement with discourse - the writer is not drawing on sources to back up what they are saying. This is different from presentation, which concerns formatting issues like incorrect citation style.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what kind of problem it is when evidence is missing entirely. Is it about how the writing is expressed, how sources are formatted, or whether sources are used at all?
_incorrect.final: The correct answer is engagement with relevant discourse. When a claim has no evidence to support it, the problem is that the writer is not engaging with sources - they are making assertions without grounding them in the research. Presentation would apply if the source was cited but the format was wrong; clarity would apply if the claim itself was hard to follow. No evidence at all is an engagement problem.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Pick a recent piece of your own writing and run it through the four pillars. Which one is your weakest? What would you change first?
instruction: If you would like, jot down your thoughts below. This is for your own reflection and will not be marked. Select Submit to save your response; it will be here when you return.

title: Summary
body: The four pillars - clarity, structure, engagement with discourse, and presentation - recur in marking criteria across genres and disciplines. This lesson brought them together as a single self-review checklist. The habit to build is straightforward: before you submit any piece of writing, run it through all four lenses. Check that your sentences are clear and precise; that your paragraphs are structured with topic sentences and closing judgements; that your sources are used, not just cited; and that your presentation is consistent and correct. One quick pass through this checklist can catch issues that would otherwise cost marks - and it only takes a few minutes once the habit is formed.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: identify the register and structural conventions of the academic essay and reflective writing, and adapt your writing to whichever genre a task requires.

title: Orientation
body: Not all academic writing sounds the same, and it shouldn't. An essay argues a point using evidence from sources; a reflective piece explores what you learned from your own experience. Each genre has its own conventions, and using the wrong register can confuse your reader or cost you marks. This lesson focuses on the difference between two genres you will encounter often: the academic essay and reflective writing. You'll learn to recognise the markers that distinguish them and to check whether your draft matches the genre your task requires.

title: Concept introduction
body:
Compare these two openings on the same topic:

Group work is frequently cited as a valuable component of higher education, offering students the opportunity to develop collaborative and interpersonal skills alongside subject knowledge.

When our group started the project, I assumed everyone would contribute equally. That wasn't quite what happened.

Both are valid academic writing, but they belong to different genres. The first is essay register: third person, formal vocabulary, a citation supporting a general claim. The second is reflective register: first person, conversational phrasing, drawing on the writer's own experience as evidence.

The key markers are straightforward. Essays use third person ('researchers found', 'the evidence suggests') and build arguments from sources. Reflective writing uses first person ('I noticed', 'looking back') and treats your experience as the primary evidence. Essays make general claims; reflective pieces explore specific, personal situations. Understanding which genre you are working in - and checking that your draft matches - is the final step before submission.

title: Worked example: comparing genres
body: Here is the same underlying topic - group work - written in two different genres. Select each heading to see the passage and what makes its register appropriate for that genre.
instruction: Select each heading to compare essay and reflective register.

_items.title: Essay excerpt
_items.body: Group work is frequently cited as a valuable component of higher education, offering students the opportunity to develop collaborative and interpersonal skills alongside subject knowledge (Osei and Bramwell, 2022). However, its effectiveness depends significantly on how responsibilities are distributed within the group.

_items.title: Why essay register
_items.body: Third person, no personal pronouns. A claim supported by a citation. Formal vocabulary ('significantly', 'component'). The writer's own experience is absent - this argues a general point, not a personal one.

_items.title: Reflective excerpt
_items.body: When our group started the project, I assumed everyone would contribute equally. That wasn't quite what happened - two of us ended up doing most of the planning, and I'm still not sure why the others held back. Looking back, I think I should have set clearer roles from the start.

_items.title: Why reflective register
_items.body: First person throughout. Informal, conversational phrasing ('I'm still not sure why'). Follows the ERA structure in miniature: what happened (Experience), what it might mean (Reflect), what to do differently (the seed of Take action). No citation - the evidence is the writer's own experience, not a source.

title: Practical guidance
body:
Before you start writing, check what genre your task requires. Assignment briefs usually signal this: 'critically evaluate' or 'discuss' points to essay register; 'reflect on your experience' or 'what did you learn' points to reflective writing. If the brief is ambiguous, ask your tutor.

Once you have a draft, run a quick register check:

  1. What person is the draft written in? First person ('I') suggests reflective; third person suggests essay.
  2. What counts as evidence? Personal experience is reflective evidence; citations are essay evidence.
  3. What is the tone? Conversational phrasing suits reflection; formal vocabulary suits essays.

If your draft mixes registers - first-person anecdotes in an essay, or citations dropped into a reflection without connecting them to your experience - adjust before submission. Genre-mixing isn't always wrong, but it should be intentional, not accidental.

title: Formative check: genre register
body: Which sentence would be appropriate in a piece of REFLECTIVE writing but NOT in an academic essay?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which sentence would be appropriate in reflective writing but not in an academic essay?

_items.text: I wasn't sure how to respond, so I just went along with the group's decision.
Group cohesion has a measurable effect on task outcomes (Smith, 2021).
This report will examine the factors influencing group performance.

_feedback.correct: That's right. 'I wasn't sure how to respond, so I just went along with the group's decision' uses first person and draws on personal experience - the hallmarks of reflective register. It would be out of place in an academic essay, which argues general claims using source-based evidence rather than personal anecdotes.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the sentence that uses first person and draws on personal experience. Which one sounds like someone reflecting on what happened to them?
_incorrect.final: 'I wasn't sure how to respond, so I just went along with the group's decision' is reflective register: first person, experience-based, conversational. 'Group cohesion has a measurable effect...' is essay register, with a citation and third-person phrasing. 'This report will examine...' is formal essay register, setting up an analytical structure. Only the first sentence belongs in reflective writing.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a piece of writing you'll submit soon. Which genre does it belong to - and does your current draft match that genre's register?
instruction: If you'd like, jot down your thoughts below. This is for your own reflection and won't be marked. Select Submit to save your response; it'll be here when you return.

title: Summary
body: Academic writing is not one thing; it shifts register depending on genre. Essays argue general claims using source-based evidence, written in third person with formal vocabulary. Reflective writing explores personal experience in first person, using a more conversational tone. The markers are clear: person, evidence type, and tone. Before you submit, check what genre your task requires and whether your draft matches. If your essay sounds like a reflection, or your reflection reads like a report, adjust the register. This final check ensures that your writing does what the task asks - and that your reader knows what to expect from the first sentence.

title: Question 1
body: Which of these sentences best demonstrates the SVO (subject-verb-object) model?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which sentence best demonstrates the SVO model?

_items.text: The researcher analysed the data.
The data was analysed by the researcher.
Analysis of the data was undertaken by the researcher.

_feedback.correct: That's right. 'The researcher analysed the data' follows SVO order: subject (the researcher), verb (analysed), object (the data). This is active voice at its clearest.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the sentence where the actor comes first, followed by the action, then what's affected. That's SVO order.
_incorrect.final: 'The researcher analysed the data' follows SVO order: the researcher (subject) analysed (verb) the data (object). 'The data was analysed by the researcher' inverts this order, putting the object first - that's passive voice. 'Analysis of the data was undertaken' buries both the actor and the action in nominalisations.

title: Question 2
body: A paragraph opens with its topic sentence, then presents evidence, then closes with a sentence stating what the evidence shows. What structural principle does this follow?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What structural principle does this paragraph structure follow?

_items.text: Claim, evidence, judgement
Evidence, then claim
Claim only, without judgement

_feedback.correct: That's right. A well-structured paragraph follows claim, evidence, judgement: the topic sentence states the claim, the body provides evidence, and the close draws a conclusion about what the evidence shows.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the full sequence: what comes first, what's in the middle, and what makes the paragraph argue rather than just report?
_incorrect.final: The correct sequence is claim, evidence, judgement. 'Evidence, then claim' puts the conclusion at the start rather than the end - that inverts the structure. 'Claim only, without judgement' stops short: it states the point but never says what the evidence adds up to. The judgement at the end is what makes a paragraph argue.

title: Question 3
body: In the 'voices' technique, what is the writer's role?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: In the voices technique, what is the writer's role?

_items.text: Framing sources with their own opening claim and closing judgement
Reporting what sources say without adding commentary
Summarising sources in their own words

_feedback.correct: That's right. In the 'voices' technique, the writer's voice opens the paragraph with a claim and closes it with a judgement. The sources speak in between, but the writer frames them.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whose voice should open and close the paragraph. What makes the difference between arguing and simply reporting?
_incorrect.final: The writer's role is to frame sources with their own opening claim and closing judgement. Simply reporting what sources say - without your own opening and closing - produces a summary rather than an argument. The 'voices' technique keeps your argument in control: you open, sources speak, you close.

title: Question 4
body: A paragraph cites a source but never explains its relevance. Which pillar does this fail?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A paragraph cites a source but never explains its relevance. Which pillar does this fail?

_items.text: Engagement with relevant discourse
Clarity and precision of expression
Structure
Presentation

_feedback.correct: That's right. When a source is cited but its relevance is never explained, the problem is engagement with discourse - the writer is reporting the source without using it to support their argument.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what's missing: the source is there, but what hasn't the writer done with it?
_incorrect.final: The correct answer is engagement with relevant discourse. Citing a source without explaining why it matters means you're reporting, not engaging. Presentation would apply if the citation format were wrong; clarity would apply if the writing were hard to follow; structure would apply if the paragraph lacked a topic sentence or closing judgement. Here, the source is present but unused - that's an engagement problem.

title: Question 5
body: Which register belongs in an academic essay rather than reflective writing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which register belongs in an academic essay rather than reflective writing?

_items.text: A third-person, source-based claim
A first-person, experience-based claim
A conversational observation about what happened

_feedback.correct: That's right. Academic essays use third-person register and build arguments from sources. First-person, experience-based claims belong in reflective writing.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what distinguishes essay register from reflective register. Which uses sources as evidence? Which uses personal experience?
_incorrect.final: A third-person, source-based claim belongs in an academic essay. Essay register is third person ('the evidence suggests'), formal, and draws on sources rather than personal experience. First-person claims ('I felt', 'I noticed') and conversational phrasing are hallmarks of reflective writing, where your own experience is the evidence.
